claims.text: Melt-spinning Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 at cooling rates of 10^5–10^6 K/s produces an amorphous ribbon.
The melt-spun amorphous alloy tends to develop primary crystalline phases during slower reheating.
Ultra-fast flash annealing immediately after melt-spinning will further kinetically stabilize the amorphous state and improve thermal stability.
The proposed flash anneal uses a heating rate greater than 10^4 K/s through the critical crystallization range.
The sample should be heated from room temperature to approximately 1200–1300 K in less than one second under an inert atmosphere.
A temperature of 1200–1300 K is just below the alloy's melting point.
An ultra-rapid thermal ramp minimizes the effective time for atomic rearrangement and suppresses nucleation of primary non-eutectic phases.
Suppressing primary-phase nucleation preserves the disordered amorphous matrix.
The alloy has crystallization-relevant thermal events near 1126–1305 K.
Reducing time within crystallization-favorable temperature intervals limits diffusion and nucleation that would otherwise produce a multistep primary-crystallization sequence.
Rapid heating can effectively freeze in the amorphous structure originally obtained by rapid cooling.
Flash-annealed samples will retain a larger amorphous fraction than conventionally reheated samples.
Flash-annealed samples will exhibit reduced or shifted DSC crystallization exotherms relative to conventionally reheated samples.
Conventional slower reheating of the rapidly quenched alloy causes extensive primary crystallization through multiple exothermic events and produces a multiphase crystalline microstructure.
Cooling rates above 10^5 K/s yield an initially amorphous Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 structure.
Reheating rates below 10^3 K/s permit extensive primary crystallization.
Reheating rates above 10^4 K/s can bypass the alloy's crystallization windows.
